title: Peddi Is Being Re-Edited While It's Still in Theatres. The Surgery Goes Far Deeper Than Janhvi Kapoor.
excerpt: ₹366 crore worldwide. Director's public apology. A revised cut from June 13. And Netflix will stream the version that caused all the outrage in the first place.
body:
There is something genuinely unprecedented happening to Peddi right now. The biggest Telugu film of 2026, a ₹350 crore sports drama starring Ram Charan at his most muscular and Janhvi Kapoor at her most controversial — is being re-cut while audiences are still buying tickets for it. Not trimmed. Not tweaked. Surgically re-edited, scene by scene, character by character, with a fresh censor certificate and a revised version that started screening on June 13, barely nine days after the original hit screens.

And the most fascinating part? When the film eventually lands on Netflix, subscribers will get the version that started all the trouble. This duality in the film's release will be particularly interesting for NRI audiences who often seek to engage with Indian cinema from abroad, as they will have access to the original, unedited version that sparked the controversy.

The Cut That Goes Deeper Than Anyone Expected

The public conversation has centered almost entirely on Janhvi Kapoor. And fair enough — the objectification of her character Achiyamma was the flashpoint that turned a box office victory lap into a full-scale industry reckoning. The camera's treatment of her body, the costuming choices, the romantic sequences that felt more predatory than playful — audiences called it out in real time, and they weren't wrong.

But according to Variety India, the re-edit extends well beyond Kapoor's scenes. Director Buchi Babu Sana is presiding over a far more comprehensive surgical operation:

  • Janhvi Kapoor's scenes featuring overt sexualization are being clipped entirely
  • Divyendu Sharma's expletives and sexual innuendo are being left on the cutting room floor
  • Shiva Rajkumar's flashback sequences as wrestling mentor Gournaidu in the second half are being shortened
  • Ram Charan and Jagapathi Babu's scenes together are being re-edited
  • Boman Irani's portions as an Indian Olympics Association member are expected to be cut

This isn't a director removing a few frames. This is a film being restructured while it's still earning money.

"It Was Never Our Intention"

Buchi Babu Sana's apology, posted on X, reads like a filmmaker genuinely blindsided by the reaction to his own film.

**"## "It Was Never Our Intention"

Buchi Babu Sana's apology, posted on X, reads like a filmmaker genuinely blindsided by the reaction to his own film."**

"As a filmmaker, I believe cinema should entertain, inspire, and connect with audiences. It should never make anyone feel uncomfortable or disrespected. We have heard the feedback regarding certain scenes in Peddi and have taken it seriously." — Buchi Babu Sana

He went further: "I have always had immense respect for women, both on and off screen, and it was never our intention to objectify or disrespect any female character."

The statement is earnest enough. But the gap between intention and execution is precisely what audiences are interrogating. You don't accidentally write scenes that reduce a female lead to decoration. You don't inadvertently frame shots that center a woman's body while her dialogue vanishes. These are choices made by an entire production apparatus — writer, director, cinematographer, editor — and the fact that nobody flagged them before release is perhaps the most damning detail of all.

Janhvi's Silence — And That Instagram Like

Kapoor herself has said nothing publicly. Ram Charan hasn't either. But in a move that speaks louder than any press statement, Janhvi reportedly liked an Instagram post that described Peddi as "the most expensive disrespect to an actress" in Indian cinema history. The like has since disappeared, but screenshots circulated widely before it vanished.

!Janhvi Kapoor — Photo: Wikimedia Commons

Veteran Telugu actress Gayatri Chaganti added fuel when she commented publicly that Kapoor "sexualises every character" through her costumes, adding, "No one is hiring her for her acting chops." Singer Sumangaly called Janhvi a "mere prop" in the film.

The pile-on reveals something uncomfortable about how the industry processes this kind of controversy. Kapoor is being held responsible for choices that were the director's to make. She showed up, performed what was asked of her, and is now absorbing criticism for a male gaze she didn't create.

Just days before release, she was all nerves and excitement — her bio still reads "#Peddi trailer and first single out now":

https://www.instagram.com/reel/DZEzK5yIKjL/

The Netflix Wrinkle

Here's where it gets genuinely interesting for the diaspora. Variety India reports that when Peddi arrives on Netflix after its theatrical run, it will be the original unedited version — the one with all the scenes that made audiences uncomfortable, all the innuendo that's being cut from theatres, all the flashbacks that are being shortened.

So Indian moviegoers who buy tickets today will see a sanitised version. NRI audiences streaming it later at home will see the film that caused the controversy. This split not only highlights the cultural differences in how films are received but also raises questions about how remittances and family ties influence viewing preferences among the diaspora. Many NRIs may find themselves discussing the film's themes and controversies with family back home, further bridging the gap between cultures.

₹366 Crore and Counting

None of this has stopped people from showing up. Peddi has crossed ₹366 crore worldwide in nine days, making it the highest-grossing South Indian film of 2026 and Ram Charan's biggest solo hit, surpassing the lifetime collections of Ala Vaikunthapurramuloo. The Telugu heartland has been the engine — the APTG market alone contributed over ₹163 crore — while the Hindi belt has added a solid ₹20 crore gross.

But the makers know that a tighter cut could unlock more from North India, where the film's 2-hour-50-minute runtime and regional pacing have been cited as barriers. The re-edit isn't just about social accountability. It's business strategy dressed as conscience.

Ram Charan's journey to this number is worth noting. After the global phenomenon of RRR, both Acharya and Game Changer underperformed. Peddi's commercial validation matters enormously for his solo-star standing — which makes the controversy all the more complicated. The numbers say triumph. The conversation says something else entirely.

What This Means

Indian cinema has never done this before — not at this scale, not this quickly, not while a film is actively making money. Bollywood has cut scenes after censor objections, sure. Directors have released "director's cuts" years later. But a mid-theatrical re-edit driven entirely by audience backlash, with a fresh censor certificate and a hard launch date for the revised version? That's new.

And it sets a precedent that cuts both ways. On one hand, it suggests that audiences now have genuine power to shape what plays in theatres. On the other, it means any film with a vocal enough opposition could face the same treatment — and the line between accountability and mob censorship is thinner than anyone wants to admit.

For now, Peddi exists as two films. The original, preserved in amber for Netflix. And the revised version, playing to packed houses across the country, slightly shorter, slightly cleaner, and carrying the weight of a very public correction.

Which one audiences remember will say more about Indian cinema in 2026 than any box office number.
